prize_parts.citation: For a poetry that has remade the Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained argument with the inherited tradition, together with the poetics that informs it.

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged, but the citation is narrower than in round 1. I now anchor it in the poetry and treat the criticism only as the poetics that informs the verse. Colleagues in both camps, and the chair's questions, pushed me to separate the quality of the poems from the critical influence. I still hold Adonis first on the criteria that bear on a whole authorship: distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, and imaginative and intellectual depth. Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses are the works the list names. As I understand public knowledge, the later decades include a very long poem-book, The Book (Al-Kitab), and a body of essays on Arabic poetics. I have not verified how well those later works sustain the early achievement, and I say so below. My claim is that a poet who reworked the idiom of a literary tradition across decades has given us a body of work that can be judged as a whole now. I do not count the fact that three members opened with him as merit. The reasoning has to hold on its own, and where it overlaps with Olsson's and Carlberg's I treat that as shared premises, not independent confirmation. The Swedish Academy's own phrase for what is rewarded, a whole authorship and not a single work, is the standard I apply. In this case that standard favours a body of work whose effect on a language and its tradition is already visible.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the core of the claim lies in prosody, diction and allusion that translation conveys only partially. My judgement rests on translations and secondary accounts, and I have not independently verified the corpus. A second reservation is that the record before the committee says little about whether the later decades deepen the project or repeat it. I raised this in round 1, and the chair's first question puts it to me directly. I can answer it only provisionally, from public knowledge of the later long poem and the essays. I cannot show it from the supplied record. If the committee cannot establish from the poems themselves that the achievement holds, the essays should not carry the case. In that situation Cărtărescu would be the more defensible recommendation, because the large prose works are more directly available to us. I would support B046 as a final recommendation if that confidence is not reached. I would not favour P000 merely because the originals are not directly readable to us. That limit applies to every shortlisted writer who does not write in a language the committee reads, and it argues for careful reading, not for refusing to decide.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg replied that 'remains to be tested' should not be a reason to defer on Cărtărescu if the central books already carry the case, and that a decades-old, still-widening oeuvre can be assessed on its established major works. He also argued that large narrative architecture survives partial translation loss better than prosodic and intertextual effects, as a point about assessability and not about greater merit.
responses.response: I accept his correction. In round 1 I used the durability of Cărtărescu's whole as a reason for ranking him below Adonis. It is a weighting argument, not a disqualification, and I would not defer on that ground alone. If the committee finds the central books carry the case, I could support him. I do not accept the assessability point in full. I think it is true for plot and structure, but the density of the sentences is exactly the feature that the case for him praises. I would apply the same discipline to both candidates: say plainly which parts of each judgement rest on translation. The difference that remains between us is what I weigh more heavily. I still give more weight to the transformation of a poetic language than to a large imaginative architecture built within an existing novelistic tradition, and I hold that as a literary weighting, not a certainty.

responses.point: Mattson says she ranked Can Xue seventh because she shared my doubt about repetition of a signature mode. She says the same objection does not apply in the same way to Cărtărescu, whose project moved through poetry, the Blinding cycle and Solenoid. She places Adonis third and says she would not oppose him if the committee can establish what in the poems is distinct from the importance of the renewal.
responses.response: Her question about Can Xue is the one I put to myself, and I cannot settle it from a partial translated selection. For that reason I keep her as my second alternative and not as a lead candidate. I agree with Mattson on the test for Adonis: what is distinct in the poems, apart from the importance of the renewal. My answer is limited. The longlist names myth, fragmentation and an argument with inherited forms, and those are features of the poems and not only of his influence. I cannot demonstrate it line by line in Arabic. Her point that the Cărtărescu project moves across forms is fair, and it is part of why he stays my first alternative. I would not claim the movement from poetry to prose shows deepening unless the later volumes are read book by book, as Sem-Sandberg proposes.

responses.point: In the chair's round-1 position and in the round-1 questions for B004 supporters, Olsson asks which collections after the early period show that Adonis's later decades deepen the project rather than repeat it. He also asks whether the citation should be anchored in the poetry alone, with the essays described only as the poetics, and what the committee does about the prosodic core being untestable in translation.
responses.response: On the citation, I now agree with him and with Carlberg. My new wording credits the poetry and names the poetics as the thing that informs it, which keeps critical influence from becoming a second ground for the prize. On the later decades, I cannot name the collections with confidence from the supplied record. The longlist names only two early and middle works, and my knowledge of the later long poem and the essays is public and unverified. I therefore treat the sustained-quality question as unresolved for me, and I have said that it is the weak point of my position. On the prosodic core, my answer is that the committee should say openly in any recommendation which parts of the judgement rest on translations and secondary accounts. Where I would push back is on any suggestion that this makes the Arabic case uniquely uncertain. Cărtărescu's density, Carson's hybrid forms and Can Xue's method each depend on something translation or format loses, and none of us reads all of the originals.

responses.point: Palm answered my Carson question by saying that the classical engagement is a through-line of method across poetry, essay, translation and verse-novel, which argues for an architecture and not a string of experiments. She concedes that book-object works such as Nox are hardest to judge from text alone and says she would weight the verbal and narrative achievement over the object form.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it has shifted my view somewhat. A through-line of method across genres is a better answer than I expected, and weighting the verbal and narrative work over the object form is the right discipline. I have not moved her above Adonis, though. Her reply asserts the through-line but does not name works beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox that would let the committee test it. The chair's question to her asks the same thing. I would also keep her translation point in mind: if translation is part of the claimed achievement, the committee would be crediting work outside the genres listed for the entry, and the citation scope would need to be settled before any vote. I still read Carson as a serious candidate whose breadth I cannot yet judge, not as a considered rejection.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis first, would anchor the citation in the poetry with the essays as the informing poetics, and keeps Cărtărescu as first alternative. She says her view rests on whether a case is established or still consolidating. She also says any committee judgement should state openly which parts rest on translations.
responses.response: I agree with her on the citation and on the need to be candid about translation, and my revised wording follows her approach. I would add one caution about the established-versus-consolidating distinction. A case being established in critical reception is not the same as the poems having been shown to be of the first rank, and I have tried to keep those apart. My round-1 statement that the essays cannot carry the case alone is the same point from the other side. I would not want my agreement with Carlberg and Olsson to be read as a bloc view. Each of us has to be able to defend the claim from the work, and I have given the limits of my own evidence above.

uncertainties: How much of the formal achievement in Arabic prosody, diction and intertextual allusion survives translation, and therefore how reliable any non-Arabic reading of Adonis is. I cannot independently verify translation quality or corpus coverage.

Whether the later decades of Adonis, including the long poem-book and the essays as I understand them from public knowledge, deepen the project or repeat it. The supplied record does not settle this and my own knowledge is unverified.
How the poetics and essays should be weighted against the poems. My revised citation treats them as informing the poetry and not as a second credit, but the committee has not agreed on this.
Whether Cărtărescu's later volumes keep intensity and moral and emotional range, and whether his poetry changes the picture of the whole oeuvre. I cannot test this from the record.

Whether Can Xue's method develops or repeats over a large output, and whether Carson's oeuvre beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox forms a consistent architecture. My knowledge of both is partial and thin.

My assessments draw on public knowledge and the supplied longlist descriptions. They do not rest on an independently verified reading of any full corpus. This is a simulated committee recommendation, not the Academy's decision, and Carlberg's vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents that I serve with Olsson, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm on the committee, and that Mattson and I were elected in the same renewal round. It records no personal, professional or financial connection to Adonis or any other shortlisted writer. My own literary practice is context and not evidence of a preference. Conflicts are disclosed here, not adjudicated.
